sources.note: Asks whether a published internal signal for code correctness is a property of the model or of the one extraction recipe used to find it, sweeps every design choice systematically, and finds no configuration is best anywhere -- with the benchmark deciding which choice wins, and a mismatched fitting source able to drive the signal below chance.
sources.title: On the Robustness of LLMs' Internal Representation of Code Correctness

sources.note: Traces the brittleness of multimodal RLVR gains under paraphrase and template change to two properties of the standard objective -- a binary verifier that cannot distinguish a wrong answer from a misformatted one, and a training distribution covering a thin slice of the prompts a deployed model meets -- and fixes both with a trinary reward and an invariance penalty across semantically equivalent prompts.
sources.title: Improving Generalization Robustness of Multimodal RLVR

sources.note: Calibrates feature-based data-contamination detectors against the systematic feature shifts that post-training introduces, by measuring how controlled prompt variants move scores on known non-members and then correcting only the recurring shift directions, with the gains concentrated at the low-false-positive operating point rather than in AUC.
sources.title: Calibrating Post-Training Feature Shifts for LLM Data Contamination Detection

sources.note: Reads a frozen vision-language model's forward pass as a structured computational trace -- a graph over image patches, query tokens and generated tokens with attention as edges, processed by interleaved relational, spatial and sequential modules -- and shows that structuring the same internals prior detectors already read lifts hallucination detection from a 69-75 AUC plateau to 90.
sources.title: UniProbe: A Learnable Token-Level Hallucination Detector for Large VLMs using Multi-Structural Internal Representations

sources.note: Trains self-correction as a step-level preference problem -- preferring a detect-and-repair continuation over the continuation that would follow if the error went unaddressed -- after first initialising with ordinary step-level preference optimisation, and finds that correcting more often and detecting more errors both anti-correlate with accuracy.
sources.title: Reinforcing Step-level Reasoning for Effective Self-Correction in LLMs

instructions:
Write the wiki definition for 'distribution shift'.

The sources below are every archived paper and talk that mentions it. Define it as they use it: if they disagree, say so; if the term is used loosely, say that too.

`related` is the one part of the note nothing can work out on its own. The wiki already links entities that turn up in the same summary; what it cannot see is the neighbour a reader would actually want next — the generation before this one, the benchmark it was built to beat, the method it replaces. Name those. Leave the list empty rather than repeating what the sources already put side by side.

Rules:
- Write in en.
- Ground every statement in the supplied material. If something is not stated,
  leave the field empty rather than inferring it.
- No marketing language. Prefer the specific number over the adjective.
- Return one JSON object matching the schema exactly. No prose around it.

aliases: string - other names the sources use for the same thing
output_schema.definition: string - two to four sentences defining the entity as the cited sources use it, not as a textbook would
output_schema.kind: string - one of: concept, method, dataset, model
related: string - name of a neighbouring entity worth linking to. Kept as you give it and never derived away, so name what a reader should turn to next rather than what happens to appear alongside this. Answering again replaces the whole list; an empty list retracts

result.definition: A difference between the distribution a model was trained on and the one it meets, used across 5 sources in two distinct senses the archive keeps apart. The training sense is the train-inference mismatch that on-policy methods exist to remove: learning from a teacher corpus leaves the student unprepared for its own prefixes, and supervised self-correction suffers it in a specific way, biasing the model toward following correction templates rather than selectively revising real errors. The evaluation sense is what a deployed model meets, where the archive's material is about detecting the shift rather than surviving it -- guarded captions retaining 95.4 percent of vanilla word count with only a small distribution shift is how one source rules out suppression as the mechanism for its improvement. One further instance from the corpus: flow-based methods that swap a deterministic sampler for a stochastic one during training optimise samples the test-time sampler does not produce, which is the same problem stated in continuous space.
